params.require: a3 != a1 or b3 != b1 or q3 != q1
params.why: the third distractor must be a different function from the first

params.require: a3 != a2 or b3 != b2 or q3 != q2
params.why: the third distractor must be a different function from the second

stem: Exactly one of the following exponential functions has no $x$-intercept. Which one?
solution: To find an $x$-intercept we let $y=0$. For $y=a\cdot b^{x}+q$ this gives $a\cdot b^{x}=-q$, so $b^{x}=-\frac{q}{a}$.
A power of a positive base is always positive. So there is an $x$-intercept only if $-\frac{q}{a}$ is positive; if it is negative, the equation has no solution.
For $y={=a1}\cdot {=b1}^{x}{=signed(q1)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b1}^{x}={=c1}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a2}\cdot {=b2}^{x}{=signed(q2)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b2}^{x}={=c2}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a3}\cdot {=b3}^{x}{=signed(q3)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b3}^{x}={=c3}$. This is positive, so there is an $x$-intercept.
For $y={=a0}\cdot {=b0}^{x}{=signed(q0)}$: setting $y=0$ gives ${=b0}^{x}={=c0}$. This is negative, and no power of ${=b0}$ is negative, so there is no solution.

proposed_misconceptions.label: A positive a keeps the graph above the x-axis
proposed_misconceptions.description: Decides that a graph with a > 0 stays above the x-axis and so has no x-intercept, ignoring that a negative constant q shifts the graph down far enough to cross the axis.

proposed_misconceptions.label: A negative a keeps the graph below the x-axis
proposed_misconceptions.description: Decides that a graph with a < 0 stays below the x-axis and so has no x-intercept, ignoring that a positive constant q shifts the graph up far enough to cross the axis.

proposed_misconceptions.label: b^x is never zero, so there is no x-intercept
proposed_misconceptions.description: Reasons that y = ab^x + q can never equal 0 because b^x is never 0, carrying the 'no x-intercept' of y = ab^x over to every exponential function and forgetting that q can cancel ab^x.

notes: Advanced: the objective's 'recognise when there is no x-intercept'. The parent figure (ex6-8-48a, y = 2^x and y = -2^x) shows two exponential graphs that never meet the x-axis. Here q is not zero: setting y = 0 gives b^x = -q/a, which has a solution only when -q/a > 0, that is when a and q have opposite signs. Exactly one option (a and q of the same sign) has no x-intercept; the other three have a and q of opposite signs, so each has one. The stem never changes, so distinct_by_choices is set; the options vary over 5 x 9 x 4 numbers for each of four functions. Distractor 1 (a > 0, q < 0) and distractor 2 (a < 0, q > 0) carry the sign-of-a errors; distractor 3 takes either sign pattern and carries the general 'b^x is never 0' error. Option texts are the four formulas, so a blind solver answers by formula.
